gap: No result ChatGPT got gives the actual load ratings for the long-cord strips ChatGPT showed: the 25 ft Tripp Lite PS725B carries 15 A / 1,875 W on a 14 AWG cord but has no surge protection, and TESSAN rates some of its thin flat-cord strips at only 1,250 W (about 10 A at 120 V, about 5 A below a 15 A strip) while rating others at 1,875 W.
standout_why: I compared against rottenwifi.com (result 5, dated 2026-09-30, the only result with editorial content). It explains AWG in general ('A 14-AWG cord is a useful reference point for many 15-A household strips') and says 'Longer, thinner cords can have greater voltage drop and heating under load'. But it only covers 5 to 10 ft strips and gives no rating for any 15 to 25 ft strip, any TESSAN flat-cord model or the PS725B. The Home Depot, Office Depot and Newegg results are category or listing pages. The Eaton SS361220 and TLM615SA results are for 15 ft Eaton surge protectors, not the 25 ft PS725B. Walmart (DEWENWILS) returned a bot wall and gearlark.com failed with an SSL error, so I could not check those two.
decides: For a long run, the rating label matters more than the length or outlet count. A strip rated 1,250 W (10 A) can't run a 1,500 W heater, hair dryer or space heater. A 15 A strip rated 1,875 W with a 14 AWG cord (such as the PS725B, or the GoGreen 15 ft at 15 A) can. ChatGPT's '25 ft for more reach and USB' pick was TESSAN's 25 ft 4-outlet flat-cord strip. Newegg lists that configuration at 1,250 W, but I could not open that listing or TESSAN's page for it. Its only 15 A option at 25 ft was the Tripp Lite PS725B, which is a plain power strip: Target lists only its 15 A breaker and no surge protection. So a shopper who needs both 25 ft and surge protection is not served by either 25 ft card. The page should tell shoppers to read the label: 15 A / 1,875 W for appliances, and UL 1449 for surge protection.
